Stage 3 · Grammar

Usual, now, or from the past until now

Three present forms, one decision.

Read these four sentences. They all come from the recording later in this lesson.
  • I get on well with a lot of people at work.
  • We’re not speaking to each other at the moment.
  • I have fallen out with one of my best friends.
  • I have known her since we were at school.
Which sentence is about something that started in the past and is still true now?
English has three ways of talking about the present, and they are not interchangeable.

Most languages have one present tense. English has three, and each of them says something different about how the action sits in time. This is the first thing to accept about the English present system: you are not choosing between a right form and a wrong one, you are choosing what you want your listener to understand.

The present simple describes what is normally, repeatedly or permanently true. When you say I get on well with my colleagues, you are not telling anybody what is happening at this second; you are describing a stable fact about your life. The present continuous describes what is in progress around now — either literally at this moment (I’m listening) or over a temporary stretch of time (He’s staying with us this month). It also describes change in progress: The internet is changing the way we behave.

The present perfect is the one learners find hardest, because it uses a past participle but is not really about the past. It is about the link between a past event and now. Sometimes that link is duration — something started earlier and is still true (I’ve known her since school). Sometimes it is experience — it happened at some unspecified point in your life and that is the point (Have you ever fallen out with a friend?). Sometimes it is a result you can still see (I’ve lost her number). What the present perfect never does is fix an event to a finished time; the moment you say yesterday or last year, English forces you into the past simple instead.

Understanding this well matters beyond accuracy. I work in Astana and I’m working in Astana both describe a job, but the first sounds permanent and the second sounds temporary. Your listener will draw conclusions from your choice of form even if you did not intend them.

Before you look at the table: the table below sorts the three forms by the question they answer — usual, now, or from the past up to now. Read the middle column first; the forms will make far more sense once you can name what each one is for.
The three forms
FormWhat it saysExampleSignal words
Present simpleusual, repeated, always trueI meet up with them after work.usually, often, every week
Present continuoushappening now, or around now and changingWe are not speaking at the moment.now, at the moment, currently
Present perfectstarted in the past, still true or still counting nowI have known him for ten years.for, since, ever, never, lately
Present perfectfinished, but the time is not finishedShe has sent three messages this week.today, this week, already, yet

The decision, in one question. Is it usual, is it now, or does it run from the past up to now? Usual takes the present simple. Now takes the present continuous. From the past up to now takes the present perfect.

For and since recycled mark how long. Use for with a length of time (for ten years, for a week) and since with the point it started (since 2019, since we were at school).

The mistake to avoid. English does not use the present simple with for or since: not I know her since 2019 but I have known her since 2019. And know is a state, so it is never I am knowing.

One more. A finished time takes the past simple, not the present perfect: I met him last year, but I have already met him.

Now say it. Make three sentences about your own friends, one in each form.

Say them out loud: one usual, one about right now, one with for or since.Say them to your teacher: one usual, one about right now, one with for or since.Say them to your partner: one usual, one about right now, one with for or since.

Full grammar reference — present simple, present continuous and present perfect

What it is

These are the three verb forms English uses to talk about the present. They are not three ways of saying the same thing: each one places the action differently in time. The present simple describes what is generally or repeatedly true; the present continuous describes what is in progress around the moment of speaking; the present perfect connects a past event to the present moment.

What it means, and what it does

Choosing between them is a choice about perspective, not about when something objectively happened. I work in Astana presents a job as a permanent fact. I’m working in Astana presents the same job as temporary. I’ve worked in Astana presents it as experience that counts up to now. The grammar carries meaning the words alone do not.

When and why we use it

Most languages have one present tense. English has three, and each of them says something different about how the action sits in time. This is the first thing to accept about the English present system: you are not choosing between a right form and a wrong one, you are choosing what you want your listener to understand.

The present simple describes what is normally, repeatedly or permanently true. When you say I get on well with my colleagues, you are not telling anybody what is happening at this second; you are describing a stable fact about your life. The present continuous describes what is in progress around now — either literally at this moment (I’m listening) or over a temporary stretch of time (He’s staying with us this month). It also describes change in progress: The internet is changing the way we behave.

The present perfect is the one learners find hardest, because it uses a past participle but is not really about the past. It is about the link between a past event and now. Sometimes that link is duration — something started earlier and is still true (I’ve known her since school). Sometimes it is experience — it happened at some unspecified point in your life and that is the point (Have you ever fallen out with a friend?). Sometimes it is a result you can still see (I’ve lost her number). What the present perfect never does is fix an event to a finished time; the moment you say yesterday or last year, English forces you into the past simple instead.

Understanding this well matters beyond accuracy. I work in Astana and I’m working in Astana both describe a job, but the first sounds permanent and the second sounds temporary. Your listener will draw conclusions from your choice of form even if you did not intend them.

Typical situations

You will need all three constantly in ordinary conversation: describing your routine and your relationships, saying what is going on at the moment, explaining a temporary arrangement, describing something that is changing, and saying how long you have known somebody or done something. Almost any conversation about your own life will move between the three within a few sentences.

  • Habits and routines — actions that happen regularly, whether or not they are happening at this moment.We meet up after work from time to time.
  • Permanent situations and general truths — facts about the world, or about you, that are not expected to change.Most people have about five close friends. Water boils at 100°C.
  • Actions in progress now — something happening at the moment of speaking, or around it.Sorry, I can’t talk — I’m meeting a client.
  • Temporary situations — something true just now but not permanently.She’s living with her parents while she looks for a flat.
  • Changing situations — a trend or development in progress, often with more and more, increasingly, get + comparative.The internet is changing the way our brains work.
  • Unfinished time up to now — a state or situation that began in the past and is still true, with for or since.I’ve known her since we were at school.
  • Experience, with no time stated — the fact that something has happened at some point in your life; when is not the point.Have you ever fallen out with a close friend?
  • Finished action inside unfinished time — the action is over but the time period is not.She’s sent me three messages today.

How it differs from similar structures

for or since? for + a length of time (for three months, for years) · since + the point it started (since March, since we were at school).
Present perfect or past simple? If the time is finished (yesterday, last week, in 2019), use the past simple. If the time is unfinished or unstated, use the present perfect. Lesson 14 returns to this contrast in detail.

How to build it

Present simple: subject + base verb (+ -s / -es for he, she, it)
Present continuous: subject + am / is / are + verb-ing
Present perfect: subject + have / has + past participle
Present simple — affirmativeI / you / we / they meet · he / she / it meets
Present simple — negativeI don’t meet · she doesn’t meet
Present simple — questionDo you meet…? · Does she meet…?
Present continuous — affirmativeI am meeting · you are meeting · he is meeting
Present continuous — negativeI am not meeting · they aren’t meeting
Present continuous — questionAre you meeting…? · Is she meeting…?
Present perfect — affirmativeI have known · she has known
Present perfect — negativeI haven’t known · he hasn’t known
Present perfect — questionHave you known…? · Has she known…?
Short answersYes, I do. / No, she isn’t. / Yes, we have. — never repeat the main verb.

Spelling and word order

  • Third person -s: add -es after -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o (watches, goes); consonant + y becomes -ies (study → studies), but vowel + y just adds -s (play → plays).
  • -ing: drop a silent -e (make → making); double a final consonant after one stressed vowel (get → getting, begin → beginning); -ie becomes -y (lie → lying).
  • Regular past participles end in -ed and follow the same doubling rule (stop → stopped). Irregular participles must be learnt as a set: know — knew — known, meet — met — met, fall — fell — fallen.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • In speech the auxiliary is almost always contracted: I’m, she’s, they’re, I’ve, he’s. Full forms sound emphatic or formal.
  • ’s can be is or has. The word after it tells you which: She’s working (= is) but She’s worked (= has).
  • The have in have been is usually weak and almost disappears: I’ve been sounds like /aɪv bɪn/. Learners often fail to hear it, which is why the form seems to vanish in natural speech.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • State verbs (know, believe, understand, own, belong, prefer, mean, recognize) describe conditions rather than activities and are normally not used in the continuous, in any tense. This is developed fully in Lesson 2.
  • The present continuous is also used for fixed future arrangements: I’m meeting them later tonight. The form is present; the meaning is future.
  • With always, the present continuous expresses irritation at a repeated action: He’s always losing his phone. Compare the neutral He always loses his phone.
  • British English prefers the present perfect with just, already and yet (I’ve just seen him); American English often uses the past simple (I just saw him). Both are correct in their own variety.
  • Been and gone are not the same: She’s been to Almaty (she went and came back) but She’s gone to Almaty (she is still there).

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I know her since 2019. → I have known her since 2019.Since measures from the past up to now, so it needs the present perfect.
  • I am knowing him for years. → I have known him for years.Know is a state verb: no continuous, and for needs the perfect.
  • We are meeting up every Friday. → We meet up every Friday.A regular routine takes the present simple, not the continuous.
  • I have seen him last week. → I saw him last week.Last week is finished time, so the past simple is required.
  • She don’t socialize much. → She doesn’t socialize much.Third person singular takes doesn’t, and the main verb then stays in the base form.
  • How long you know her? → How long have you known her?Questions need the auxiliary before the subject.

More examples in context

  • routineI get on well with almost everyone at work.
  • general truthPeople lose touch when they change jobs.
  • nowBe quiet for a second — I’m listening to this.
  • temporaryHe’s staying with us until his flat is ready.
  • trendMore and more people are keeping in touch only online.
  • arrangementWe’re meeting at the café at seven.
  • unfinished timeThey’ve been friends since university.
  • experienceHave you ever fallen out with a close friend?
  • result nowI can’t call her — I’ve lost her number.
  • inside this weekShe’s sent me three messages this week.

A tip for remembering it

Ask yourself one question before you choose: usual, now, or from the past up to now? Usual → present simple. Now → present continuous. From the past up to now → present perfect. If a time word is present, let it decide for you: every week pulls the simple, at the moment pulls the continuous, for / since / ever / yet pull the perfect.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Present simple = usual, repeated, permanently true.
  2. Present continuous = in progress now, temporary, or changing — and also a fixed future arrangement.
  3. Present perfect = a link between past and present: unfinished time, life experience, or a present result.
  4. For + how long, since + when it started; both take the present perfect.
  5. A finished time expression (yesterday, last year) forces the past simple, never the present perfect.
  6. State verbs such as know and believe do not take the continuous.
